Subject: SLO handoff: context sizes, streaming needs, and throughput targets

Hi Priya / Amit —

Thanks again for the demo earlier. Quick recap and the next steps we agreed on, so we have alignment before I loop in the infra team:

- Goal: Apply Redwood to BankCorp’s real-time compliance summarization pipeline. Expected steady-state queries: ~200 qps at peak; nightly batch reprocessing ~5M tokens/hour.
- Targets you mentioned on the call: 95th pct latency = 150ms for short responses (<=128 tokens out), soft target 300ms for longer outputs (up to 1k output tokens) when streaming is acceptable.
- Context window: primary inputs vary 2k–16k tokens (combination of customer chat + metadata + legal snippets). Top priority is keeping short-turn latency tight for live UX; for large context runs, throughput/cost is important and some additional latency is acceptable.

Action items we discussed:
1) Vendor/Redwood to confirm whether we can meet the 150ms 95th for the short-response class (with batching disabled or minimal batching).
2) Redwood to surface latency estimates for different context window sizes (2k / 8k / 16k) including streaming vs non-streaming modes.
3) BankCorp to share a sample prompt + average token breakdown (input vs expected output) and clarify which flows must be streaming.
4) Set follow-up technical sync (engineers only) next week to validate KV cache and batching configs.

I attached a lightweight SLO requirements matrix that would help us capture the flows. I’ll also route this to Rishi and Dev internally for an initial feasibility note.

Thanks —
Vanessa Ortiz

Thanks Vanessa — useful recap. A couple clarifications from our side:

- The 150ms 95th is for the “fast search & snippet” flow where the user sees a single-line justification (<=40 tokens). These are extremely latency-sensitive.
- The 300ms soft target applies to the assistant-style replies around 200–400 tokens when we stream token-by-token client-side.
- For the long-context legal assembly flow (up to 16k), we can tolerate up to ~2s P95 if the output is batched overnight or the client is explicitly in a deferred job.

We’ll share a sample JSON payload with token counts by 5pm PT today. Also, BankCorp is particularly interested in whether prefix caching / KV cache can reduce repeated context overhead (we often resend policy headers).

—Amit

Vanessa / team / Priya / Amit —

Short answer: we can plausibly meet the 150ms P95 for the <=40-token fast snippets in a non-batched, low-concurrency lane using optimized runtime kernels and MPS/FP16 instances with prefix caching. Caveats below with rough ballpark numbers (P95) for a single-request path (no cross-request batching), assuming a reasonably tuned dedicated GPU instance: 

- 2k context (input ~1.5k tokens, 40-token output): ~90–140ms P95 (streaming off; single-shot return).
- 8k context (input ~6.5k tokens, 40-token output): ~140–220ms P95 (prefix KV cache reduces cost when policy header repeated).
- 16k context (input ~13k tokens, 40-token output): ~220–420ms P95 (cache helps but memory bandwidth and KV lookups add cost).

For streamed outputs (200–400 tokens) where client consumes token-by-token:
- 2k context: ~180–280ms P95 to deliver first N tokens and steady stream thereafter (initial token latency higher due to generation startup).
- 8k context: ~300–550ms P95 initial; incremental token latency ~3–8ms per token depending on instance and quantization.
- 16k context: ~500–1200ms P95 initial, incremental token latency similar to 8k but overall higher because of larger KV and attention cost.

Notes / configuration knobs we recommend for BankCorp flows:
1) KV / prefix caching: enable for policy headers and repeated prompts. This reduces per-request prep and can move a worst-case 16k P95 down ~20–30% for short outputs.
2) Two serving lanes: "fast-lane" (no batching, dedicated small batch size, higher cost) for <=40-token responses; "bulk-lane" (controlled batching, relaxed latency SLOs) for long-context or nightly jobs.
3) Streaming optimization: start-generation prefetching and smaller generation chunks to reduce first-token latency. Provide a small HTTP SSE/protocol buffer client that can accept chunked outputs.
4) Quantization / instance sizing: use mixed-precision and tuned kernels; for 8k/16k we recommend >=A100-class or equivalent with host memory pinned to avoid KV paging.
5) Concurrency guidance: to keep P95 stable, cap concurrency per GPU for the fast-lane (we recommend <=8 concurrent fast requests per GPU for the 150ms target).

I’ll produce a short tech note with these numbers and a config suggestion by EOD. If they can share the sample payload Amit mentioned, I’ll run a small on-prem micro-benchmark and return measured P95s for at least the 2k and 8k cases.

—Rishi
